claims.text: The as-cast high-entropy alloy has a highly disordered, random distribution of constituent elements.
Controlled annealing can induce partial atomic ordering in the alloy without causing phase separation or compositional segregation.
Partial atomic ordering governs the emergence of superconductivity in the annealed alloy.
The relevant superconducting test regime is below approximately 10 K.
Annealing produces locally ordered clusters or atomic-scale regions with reduced compositional randomness.
Local atomic order increases the density of states at the Fermi level.
Local atomic order strengthens electron-phonon interactions.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling compensates for disorder-induced scattering in the dirty limit.
The alloy is expected to support conventional BCS-type Cooper pairing in the dirty limit.
Annealed samples will have a higher superconducting critical temperature than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will exhibit sharper superconducting transitions in specific-heat and magnetization measurements than as-cast samples.
Annealed samples will have a greater superconducting volume fraction than as-cast samples.
The fully disordered as-cast state is expected to show little or very weak superconductivity under the same low-temperature conditions.
The proposed mechanism should apply to high-entropy alloys with similar elemental mixtures and disordered structures.
The mechanism may not apply when constituent elements provide strong intrinsic pairing.
Annealing-induced phase segregation can limit or invalidate the proposed mechanism.
The amount of local ordering needed to affect electron-phonon coupling in high-entropy alloys is not established.
Specific-heat measurements can be used to estimate electron-phonon coupling strength in the tested samples.
